newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori hit by resignations, protests.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori hit by resignations, protests.

text.p: Street protests and three cabinet resignations piled pressure on Thursday on Peru's embattled President Alberto Fujimori, who is facing the most serious opposition of his seven years in power.
Around five thousand workers, teachers and students fought their way through police lines and marched towards the presidential palace chanting "Down with the dictatorship."
Demonstrators clashed with police as they pushed through side-streets into the main square opposite the palace. Some fought with sticks and metal wires while others tossed rocks and bottles.
Four lines of about 500 heavily-armed riot police guarded the palace, where Fujimori was present, while soldiers stood on the roof and a police helicopter flew overhead.
The protest, one of the largest against Fujimori since he took office in 1990, lasted about two hours and followed the resignation of three ministers from Fujimori's cabinet.

Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela quit on Wednesday. One of the most respected figures in the cabinet, Tudela was widely believed to have resigned to disassociate himself from a string of embarrassing scandals facing Fujimori.

Defence Minister Gen. Tomas Castillo Meza also resigned over alleged rights abuses by the security forces, government sources said. His post was filled by Interior Minister Gen. Cesar Saucedo, who in turn was replaced by regional military head Gen. Jose Villanueva.

Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza also quit, and was replaced by lawyer Alfredo Quispe Correa. Completing the cabinet reshuffle, Fujimori named businessman Ludwig Meier to the vacant post of fisheries minister.
The five new ministers were sworn in late on Thursday.

The deepening political crisis has sent Fujimori tumbling to his lowest popularity level, 23 percent, on public anger over widespread poverty and allegations of corruption and rights abuses by his government and the security forces.

"It's a good thing there are Peruvians who have the dignity to reject all this ill-treatment from the Fujimori government," said Juan Jose Gorriti, secretary-general of the General Workers' Confederation that organised the protests.
Peru's military top brass gathered in the presidential palace earlier on Thursday to publicly pledge their support for Fujimori in a hastily-called ceremony.

"We want to emphatically express our subordination, loyalty and disciplined support," armed forces head Gen. Nicolas Bari de Hermoza said. "Mr. President, you can be absolutely convinced that in the armed forces and national police force, you have the firmest pillars to defend democracy and the constitution," he added.

A grave-faced Fujimori noted that he and the military had shared "seven long years" and had successfully overcome the major problems threatening Peru's stability, a reference to guerrilla warfare and economic turmoil. But he added that the country was living a "new era" and facing a new problem, an apparent reference to the growing opposition to his rule.
A survey by leading pollster Apoyo S.A. earlier this week showed that 53 percent of Peruvians believe the military is the real power in Peru. Only 38 percent said Fujimori holds the reins.
Fujimori has maintained a delicate partnership with the military since 1990, relying on their support for his war on leftist guerrillas and introduction of tough economic reforms.

Particularly damaging to Fujimori were weekend claims of phone-tapping by the secret services, and the annulment of Peruvian citizenship for Israeli-born Baruch Ivcher, owner of a local television channel that was critical of the military.
The allegation believed to have brought Meza's departure was the recent torture of army intelligence agent Leonor La Rosa by colleagues angry at her alleged leaks to the media.
